Localized, piecewise constraints — not blunt global inequalities — are what restore consistency to the theory.

Part III — Small Infrared Aerial Target Detection via Kinematic Constraints

While physicists work atomic boundaries and mathematicians work theoretical ones, remote-sensing engineers face a very different edge: pulling real signal out of the boundary of sensor noise. Small Infrared Aerial Target Detection (SIATD) underpins airborne early-warning and guidance systems — infrared offers all-weather capability, night operation, and passive concealment that optical and radar can’t match.

But detecting anything from a moving airborne platform is brutal. Fast ego-motion makes backgrounds shift violently — clouds, dense vegetation, sun-glint on water — while distant targets appear as featureless, isotropic spots just 3×3 to 7×7 pixels, with no shape or semantic content to lean on.

Why existing methods struggle

Single-frame methods (MLCM, RIPT, facet-kernel filters) assume the target has a distinctly different spatial spread or contrast than its background. They’re computationally cheap but suffer catastrophic false-alarm rates whenever the background itself contains high-frequency thermal anomalies — building edges, wave crests — that mimic small targets.

Multi-frame methods (dynamic programming, 3D spatiotemporal tensors, optical flow) correlate gray-level distributions across sequences. More robust, but computationally heavy, and they routinely fail when the platform’s own motion causes non-linear background shifts that break frame-subtraction and tensor approximations. Even CNNs struggle here — their pooling layers, built to extract high-level semantic features, wash out sub-pixel dim targets along with the rest of the background.

Stage 1 — LightGBM as a fast spatial classifier

Rather than lean on fragile contrast measures or heavy CNNs, this approach treats single-frame candidate detection as a binary classification problem solved with LightGBM — a decision-tree ensemble that uses Gradient-based One-side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) for speed suited to live video throughput.

An initial positive/negative adaptive median filter screens the image first, keeping only pixels that clear a local-intensity threshold (parameters k₁ for bright targets, k₂ for dark targets). Each surviving “interesting pixel” gets a local window (3×3 up to 15×15) flattened into a vector V, from which seven statistical features are extracted:

Fed into the LightGBM classifier, this extracts substantial statistical depth from a single frame in about 44 ms per image, with a recall of 0.90 on established benchmarks.

Stage 2 — imposing kinematic physics

Spatial candidates alone aren’t enough — separating true targets from noise means adding physics over time. First, ego-motion is compensated by registering frames with SURF keypoint extraction and a RANSAC-based homography transform, mapping all candidates to one shared coordinate space.

From there, the system leans on a simple physical truth: real targets move in smooth, inertia-governed trajectories; noise flickers randomly. Two constraints enforce this:

Short-strict constraint (trajectory growth). Over three consecutive frames, motion is assumed roughly linear. A cost function measures how far a new candidate deviates from the ideal linear projection of the prior two frames:

If C(i,j) falls below a strict threshold σ₁, and velocity stays under limit σ₂, the candidate joins the trajectory. This aggressively severs random noise from real tracks.

Long-loose constraint (trajectory merging). Dim targets may briefly drop out (occlusion, a missed classification), fragmenting trajectories. This constraint projects two broken segments’ velocity vectors into the missing gap and computes a similarity score S(T¹, T²); if it clears threshold σ₃, the segments merge — preserving one continuous track for the true target.

Any trajectory that survives these filters and persists past a dynamic length threshold, over a sliding window L, is confirmed as a real target:

The SIATD dataset — and how the method performs

Progress here was long bottlenecked by data scarcity — the prior standard, SIRST, held only 427 single-frame images, far too little for deep models to generalize rather than overfit to one background. The new SIATD dataset fixes that:

Benchmarked against current state-of-the-art (AGADM, RIPT, MLCM, TIPI, STTV-WNIPT, ASTTV-NTLA), the LightGBM-plus-trajectory method wins decisively — especially in the hardest clutter environments:

While single-frame models and tensor approximations get overwhelmed by high-frequency clutter from building edges and vegetation, imposing strict kinematic trajectory constraints aggressively filters non-linear noise — landing an overall precision near 0.92.

Conclusion

Modern applied science, across three completely different fields, keeps returning to the same exercise: mastering boundaries.

In 2D spintronics, expanding the van der Waals gap of Fe₃GaTe₂ via PMN-PT piezoelectric strain breaks in-plane crystal symmetry and weaponizes the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction — reprogramming magnetic domains with zero applied current. In geometric function theory, resolving the boundary behavior of isosceles trapezoids through localized, piecewise spatial mappings fixes a real mathematical paradox, proving quasiconformal reflection coefficients scale linearly rather than quadratically. And in computational vision, imposing strict kinematic constraints over time lets remote-sensing systems cut through severe thermal clutter and isolate dim infrared targets where deep learning and tensor methods alone fail.

The atomic Hamiltonian of a ferromagnet, the complex dilatation of a Riemann sphere, and the statistical variance of a thermal sensor have almost nothing in common on the surface. But progress in all three depends on the same discipline: defining, respecting, and precisely manipulating the constraints at the boundary.
art-sub-15:
The Impossible Triangle

Since its introduction, the Transformer has been the near-universal foundation underneath modern AI — language, vision, multimodal systems, all of it. Its self-attention mechanism lets every element of a sequence interact densely with every other element, which is exactly what makes it so good at information-dense tasks like language. But that density has a price: standard softmax attention scales quadratically with sequence length, in both compute and memory, during training.

The cost doesn’t stop at training. During autoregressive generation, a Transformer has to cache the key and value vectors for every previously generated token — the infamous KV cache — and that cache grows linearly with sequence length. In practice, this turns decoding into a memory-bandwidth-bound operation: the bottleneck isn’t how fast the GPU can compute, it’s how fast it can shuttle an ever-growing cache back and forth across the memory hierarchy. That inflates latency, power draw, and deployment cost in a way that gets worse, not better, as context windows grow.

For years, sequence modeling research has circled around what’s often called the impossible triangle: you can have training parallelism, or cheap constant-time inference, or Transformer-level modeling quality — pick two. Early attempts at sub-quadratic models — linear attention, gated convolutions, classic RNNs — usually gave up quality to get efficiency, especially on language tasks where dense token-to-token interaction seemed to matter most.

That’s changed. A new generation of architectures — Mamba, xLSTM, RetNet, and Gated Linear Attention, among others — has closed the gap, and in places surpassed it, by combining structured matrices, hardware-aware kernel design, data-dependent gating, and clever state-expansion tricks. The line between “attention model,” “recurrent network,” and “state space model” is dissolving; increasingly they’re just different computational views of the same underlying mathematics. This piece maps that landscape in depth.

1. The State Space Revolution: From Continuous Signals to Mamba

Where SSMs came from

Structured State Space Sequence Models (SSMs) started life as a genuinely different lineage from Transformers — descended from classical Kalman filters and continuous-time dynamical systems, not from attention at all. The base formulation maps a continuous signal through a hidden latent state, and a discretization step (commonly zero-order hold) converts the continuous parameters into discrete matrices usable in a neural network. The elegant part: the same underlying model can be computed two completely different ways — as a sequential recurrence (efficient, one step at a time, ideal for inference) or as a global convolution (fully parallel, ideal for training).

Early architectures built on this idea — S4, H3, Hyena — dominated benchmarks specifically built to stress long-range dependency, like the Long Range Arena, especially on continuous signal domains like audio and pixels.

The catch: Linear Time Invariance

These early SSMs shared a structural limitation called Linear Time Invariance (LTI) — the parameters governing how the hidden state evolves stay fixed across every time step, regardless of what the input actually contains. That sounds like a minor detail, but it has a serious consequence: an LTI model literally cannot do content-based reasoning. It can’t choose to pay more attention to one token because of what that token is, because its dynamics don’t depend on content at all.

This shows up starkly on synthetic tasks like Selective Copying and Induction Heads, where the position of relevant information is randomized rather than fixed. A model that treats every position with identical, input-independent dynamics simply has no mechanism to selectively compress the sequence — it has to treat everything uniformly, which means it can’t reliably remember the one token that happened to matter thirty steps ago while ignoring the twenty-nine that didn’t.

Mamba-1: breaking LTI with selection

Mamba solves this by making the core SSM parameters — the step size Δ, and the projection matrices B and C — direct, learned functions of the input itself. This “Selection Mechanism” is the whole innovation: it turns a rigid, time-invariant convolution into a flexible, time-varying recurrence that can filter out irrelevant tokens and hold onto important ones indefinitely.

The cost of that flexibility is architectural: a time-varying SSM can no longer be computed as a global convolution via FFT, which was the trick that made earlier SSMs fast to train. Mamba’s answer is a hardware-aware parallel scan — recognizing that modern GPUs are bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, not raw arithmetic, the implementation fuses the discretization and scan steps so they run entirely inside fast on-chip SRAM, only touching the much slower HBM (high-bandwidth memory) to read inputs and write final outputs. The expanded hidden state itself is never materialized in slow memory at all.

The payoff: Mamba runs up to 3× faster than prior LTI convolution-based models on A100 GPUs, while keeping linear scaling in sequence length. The architecture itself is also simpler than what came before — Mamba fuses the SSM and the Transformer’s MLP block into a single homogeneous layer, dropping attention entirely. Empirically, this wasn’t a modest result: a 3-billion-parameter Mamba model outperformed identically-sized Transformers and matched models twice its size. On the Human Genome (HG38) dataset, Mamba scaled cleanly up to context lengths of one million tokens, continuing to improve as context grew — while a baseline like HyenaDNA actually got worse on very long contexts.

Mamba-2: proving SSMs and attention are mathematical duals

Mamba-1’s scan algorithm, for all its speed, developed somewhat separately from the broader ecosystem of Transformer-optimized tooling. Mamba-2 closes that gap with a genuinely surprising theoretical result: Structured State Space Duality (SSD) — a proof that structured SSMs and a certain class of masked kernel attention are, mathematically, dual representations of the same computation.

The proof leans on the concept of semiseparable matrices: a matrix is N-semiseparable if every submatrix on or below its diagonal has rank at most N — and N here corresponds directly to the SSM’s state dimension. The core theorem: computing an SSM’s sequence transformation is exactly equivalent to multiplying by a sequentially semiseparable matrix. That equivalence unlocks two computational modes for the same model:

  • Linear (recurrent) form — O(TN) time, T = sequence length, N = state size. The classical step-by-step SSM recurrence.

  • Quadratic (dual) form — O(T²) time, by materializing the semiseparable matrix directly. Under certain parameterizations, this form is literally masked kernel attention.

Mamba-2 exploits this by splitting the sequence into chunks: the intra-chunk computation (the diagonal blocks) runs in the quadratic dual form, taking full advantage of GPUs’ highly optimized matrix-multiplication units; the inter-chunk computation (the off-diagonal, low-rank blocks) runs in the efficient linear recurrent form, passing hidden state forward between chunks. Each part runs where it’s fastest.

The result is dramatically more hardware-friendly than Mamba-1: 2–8× faster than Mamba-1’s already-optimized selective scan, and it overtakes FlashAttention-2 at sequence lengths around 2K — eventually running 6× faster at 16K. SSD also lets Mamba-2 use much larger state-expansion factors (N=64 or N=256) without the slowdowns that would have crippled earlier designs, and its refactored architecture — computing all projection matrices in parallel, echoing how Transformers generate Q/K/V together — makes it directly compatible with Megatron-style tensor parallelism, halving the synchronization overhead of Mamba-1.

2. Reimagining Linear Attention: Retention and Data-Dependent Gating

Why early linear attention underperformed

Linear attention strips softmax out of the attention computation and replaces it with feature maps on Q and K, reordering the computation via matrix associativity — the same trick underlying most of this article’s architectures. The theoretical complexity win is real, but early implementations consistently underperformed softmax attention in practice, for two related reasons: attention dilution (smooth, high-entropy attention distributions that fail to sharply distinguish relevant from irrelevant tokens) and an inability to discard stale historical information cleanly, which caused instability on long-context tasks.

RetNet: recurrence and attention, unified

The Retentive Network (RetNet) addresses this with a multi-scale retention mechanism that ties recurrence and attention together as two views of the same underlying computation, using a relative position embedding built directly into the state update. RetNet’s key move: replace softmax with a simple exponential decay factor tied to temporal distance between tokens — no learned content-dependence needed at the base level, just a clean, well-behaved decay curve.

This formulation naturally supports three distinct computational modes:

  • Parallel form — for training. The model materializes an interaction matrix combining causal masking and exponential decay, and computes the whole sequence in parallel, GPU-efficient.

  • Recurrent form — for inference. A state matrix updated one step at a time, functionally identical to a classic RNN, giving O(1) per-token decoding.

  • Chunkwise recurrent form — the balance point for very long sequences. Intra-chunk computation uses the fast parallel form; cross-chunk information passes through the recurrent form, keeping overall memory linear.

To keep this expressive across different kinds of linguistic patterns, RetNet assigns different decay rates to different attention heads — some heads specialize in tight, immediate local context, others hold onto long-range global context. Because that head-to-head variance can get large, RetNet applies GroupNorm independently per head to keep training stable.

The empirical payoff is substantial: RetNet decodes 8.4× faster than a Transformer baseline and saves 70% of GPU memory at 8K sequence length — entirely sidestepping the KV-cache problem that defines Transformer deployment cost.

Gated Linear Attention (GLA): bringing back data-dependence

RetNet’s decay is data-independent — fixed per head, not per token. Decades of RNN research says data-dependent gating (the ability to selectively forget based on content, not just recency) matters a lot. Gated Linear Attention (GLA) merges RetNet’s efficient chunkwise recurrent framework with a genuinely data-dependent gating matrix, using a low-rank parameterization to keep the added gate parameters cheap.

That data-dependence buys real expressivity, but it also breaks numerical stability in the naive parallel formulation — the cumulative product of many gates can shrink toward zero fast, an old and familiar RNN problem in a new setting. GLA’s fix is a hardware-aware algorithm with secondary-level chunking: because keeping numerical stability against vanishing gates requires additions in logarithmic space (which can’t run on standard half-precision Tensor Cores), GLA splits chunks into sub-chunks — the coarse inter-sub-chunk interactions run on fast half-precision Tensor Cores, while only the small, numerically sensitive intra-sub-chunk computations run in slower full-precision log space.

Trained at 1.3B parameters on 100B tokens of SlimPajama, GLA proved competitive with both optimized Transformers and Mamba. Its standout result is length generalization: a GLA model trained only on 2K-token contexts extrapolated cleanly to 20K-token sequences via truncated backpropagation through time, without the perplexity blowup that plagued earlier models — and it beat Mamba specifically on strict extrapolation length.

3. Resurrecting the RNN: xLSTM and HGRN2

Why the LSTM died, and what it would take to fix it

Before Transformers, the LSTM was the dominant sequence architecture — but it had three flaws that became fatal in the LLM era. First, its sigmoid gates make it mathematically bad at revising stored decisions — a problem for tasks like nearest-neighbor search, where new information sometimes needs to rapidly overwrite what was previously stored. Second, its state has to compress everything into a single scalar cell, giving it fundamentally limited storage capacity — bad news for tasks requiring high-fidelity memorization, like predicting rare tokens accurately. Third, its hidden-to-hidden recurrent connections force strictly sequential execution, making it a poor fit for GPU-scale parallelism.

xLSTM: exponential gating and matrix memory

xLSTM tackles all three problems directly. To fix the revision problem, it replaces the sigmoid input and forget gates with exponential gating — but exponentials can overflow catastrophically, so xLSTM adds a normalizer state that tracks the running product of input gates and all subsequent forget gates, keeping the whole computation numerically stable.

To address capacity and parallelization together, xLSTM introduces two distinct memory cell variants:

  • sLSTM (scalar LSTM) — keeps the scalar memory and hidden-to-hidden mixing of the classic LSTM, but with exponential gating layered on top. Uses multiple heads, mixing memory within a head but never across heads. Because of the strict sequential dependency this retains, it relies on custom, heavily-optimized CUDA kernels to stay performant.

  • mLSTM (matrix LSTM) — abandons the scalar state entirely in favor of a full matrix memory, updated via a covariance-style outer-product rule. Because it severs the hidden-to-hidden sequential dependency, mLSTM is fully parallelizable and can use the same chunkwise parallel computation strategies that power linear attention and RetNet.

Scaled to 1.3B parameters on 300B tokens of SlimPajama, xLSTM showed genuinely superior length extrapolation — maintaining low perplexity out to 16,384-token generations despite being trained on only 2,048-token sequences. On the PALOMA benchmark, which evaluates next-token prediction across 571 distinct text domains, xLSTM consistently beat RWKV-4, LLaMA, and Mamba at comparable scale — outperforming Mamba specifically in 99.5% of the evaluated domains.

HGRN2: expanding state without expanding parameters

A model’s recurrent state size is closely tied to its capacity for in-context learning — bigger state, generally, means better recall. But naively growing the state size blows up parameter count, since projection matrices scale with the square of the state dimension.

HGRN (Hierarchically Gated Linear RNN) first tackled long-range dependency by using data-dependent forget gates whose lower bounds increase monotonically layer by layer — forcing early layers to specialize in local context and later layers to specialize in long-range dependencies. But HGRN1 was still bottlenecked by a small traditional state.

HGRN2 fixes this with a genuinely elegant trick borrowed from linear attention: expand the input gate via an outer product, blowing the hidden state up into a full matrix, with the recurrent update handled through diagonalization and matrix dot products — all without introducing a single new parameter. A multi-head variant controls the resulting complexity, tying the state-expansion ratio directly to head dimension, which also means HGRN2 can borrow the same hardware-efficient chunkwise training algorithms built for GLA.

On the Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) task — a synthetic proxy specifically designed to test in-context-learning capability — HGRN2 dramatically outperformed HGRN1, confirming that parameter-free state expansion genuinely closes the memory-capacity gap that limited earlier linear RNNs.

4. Addressing Visual Modalities: Nested and Focused Attention

High-resolution images translate into sequences of thousands of patch tokens, making the quadratic cost of attention just as painful in vision as in language. Approaches like the Swin Transformer sidestep this by restricting attention to local windows — efficient, but at the cost of the global receptive field that made attention valuable in the first place. Linear attention is the obvious theoretical fix, but deploying it in vision has historically come with real accuracy costs.

Luna: pack, then unpack

Luna (Linear Unified Nested Attention) splits standard attention into two successive linear stages, using an auxiliary sequence of fixed length as a go-between. In Pack Attention, this fixed-length auxiliary sequence acts as the query, compressing the full context into a compact, fixed-size summary. In Unpack Attention, the original sequence then queries that compressed summary to pull out what it needs. Because the auxiliary sequence is generated fresh at each layer rather than being a static parameter, it absorbs context dynamically as it moves through the network.

Luna matched or beat standard Transformers on Long Range Arena tasks, and at 4K-token sequences, a Luna configuration with a projection length of just 16 required only 10% of the memory of a vanilla Transformer while running 5.5× faster.

FLatten Transformer: diagnosing two specific pathologies

The FLatten Transformer offers a more surgical diagnosis of why linear attention underperforms specifically in vision: two distinct, separable failure modes.

The focus problem. Softmax’s exponential nonlinearity naturally sharpens attention onto a small set of highly relevant regions — useful for isolating a foreground object, say. Linear attention’s distributions are comparatively smooth and diffuse — closer to averaging than to focusing. FLatten’s fix is a mapping function on Q and K that preserves vector norm but reshapes direction, pulling similar features toward shared axes and pushing dissimilar ones apart, with a scaling factor that mimics softmax’s sharper concentration.

The diversity problem. In standard attention, the attention matrix can reach full rank, equal to the number of tokens. In linear attention, rank is capped by the channel dimension per head — typically far smaller than the token count — so the attention map suffers real rank collapse, homogenizing output features. FLatten restores this with a lightweight Depthwise Convolution injected into the Value representation: because this convolution’s matrix is sparse but full-rank, it mathematically lifts the effective rank ceiling of the whole attention map back toward its theoretical maximum.

Integrated into DeiT, PVT, Swin, and CSwin backbones, FLatten Transformers delivered consistent Top-1 accuracy gains on ImageNet-1K with lower FLOPs, and up to 2.1× faster GPU inference — without sacrificing spatial reasoning quality.

5. Empirical Synthesis: Benchmarks, Scaling Laws, and Downstream Tasks

Long Range Arena and synthetic recall

Across the board, sub-quadratic architectures now dominate the Long Range Arena — the benchmark specifically designed to stress long-context reasoning:

The jump from Luna-256 to HGRN1/HGRN2 isn’t incremental — it’s a step change, roughly 25 points on average. That’s the gap between “clever efficiency trick” and “architectures with genuinely expanded state capacity.”

On MQAR (Multi-Query Associative Recall — recall a value associated with a randomly-placed key, testing raw in-context learning capacity), older models like Hyena and RWKV-4 struggled badly as the number of key-value pairs scaled up to 256. Architectures with real state expansion — xLSTM, Mamba-2, GLA — reached near-perfect accuracy instead. HGRN2’s outer-product expansion, specifically, let it thoroughly outclass HGRN1 across sequence lengths up to 512.

Zero-shot language reasoning

At real language-modeling scale, sub-quadratic models hold their own against strong Transformer baselines like Pythia and OPT:

Mamba and xLSTM are the standouts here, both beating the Pythia Transformer baseline outright at comparable scale. RetNet and GLA trail on this particular table — a useful reminder that “sub-quadratic” isn’t a single monolithic performance tier; different mechanisms for achieving linear complexity land at meaningfully different quality points, and the specific architectural choices (state expansion, gating granularity) matter as much as the complexity class.

On SlimPajama (15B and 100B token training runs), Mamba-2, xLSTM, and GLA all closely tracked or beat the perplexity curves of well-optimized LLaMA-style baselines. And on PALOMA — 571 diverse text domains — xLSTM posted the best perplexity in its class, beating Mamba in 99.5% of domains tested.

Beyond language: DNA and audio

The advantages compound in modalities where useful context naturally runs far longer than typical text. On the Human Genome (HG38) dataset, Mamba’s pretraining perplexity kept improving smoothly out to contexts of one million tokens, while HyenaDNA actually degraded past roughly 10,000 tokens — direct evidence that the selection mechanism (the ability to ignore biological noise rather than being forced to compress everything uniformly) matters, not just raw architecture efficiency.

In audio, autoregressive pretraining on the YouTubeMix piano dataset showed Mamba clearly improving on the prior state of the art (SaShiMi) for minute-long waveform contexts. On the SC09 speech-generation benchmark, a Mamba model with just 6 million parameters produced higher-fidelity audio (by Fréchet Inception Distance) than substantially larger diffusion and GAN baselines — a striking result given the parameter-count gap.

6. The System Optimization Paradigm

Hardware-awareness isn’t an implementation detail — it’s architecture

A recurring theme across every model in this piece: mathematical sub-quadratic complexity does not automatically translate into faster wall-clock performance. Early linear RNNs technically hit O(T) FLOPs but trained agonizingly slowly, because their strictly sequential, element-wise updates had low arithmetic intensity and couldn’t use GPU Tensor Cores at all. Complexity class and real-world speed are related, but they are not the same thing — and every architecture covered here treats the physical memory hierarchy of the GPU as a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought.

The consistent goal: minimize traffic to slow, high-capacity HBM, and maximize work done inside fast, small-capacity SRAM.

That shift — from O(N)-per-step, memory-hungry decoding to O(1)-per-step decoding with a fixed memory footprint — is arguably the single most consequential practical change in this entire architectural wave. It’s the difference between inference cost that grows with every token you’ve ever generated, and inference cost that simply doesn’t.

Scaling across clusters, and the rise of hybrids

To compete with frontier LLMs, these architectures also need to scale across many GPUs using established distributed-training infrastructure. Mamba-2’s refactored block — computing its parameter projections in one parallel step, mirroring how Transformers generate Q/K/V together — makes it directly compatible with Megatron-style tensor parallelism, halving synchronization overhead relative to Mamba-1.

Chunkwise algorithms also naturally support context (sequence) parallelism: because state is compressed sequentially, different chunks can run on different GPUs, with each GPU only needing to pass its final hidden state to its neighbor. That’s O(1) communication cost between GPUs — a sharp contrast to Ring Attention’s communication cost, which scales quadratically with the number of workers involved.

There’s a growing, and fairly compelling, view that the actual Pareto-optimal frontier isn’t “pure SSM” or “pure attention” but a deliberate mix of both:

Experiments combining Mamba-2’s SSD layers with a sparse sprinkling of standard softmax attention — roughly 10% of total layers — show meaningful gains in in-context learning and zero-shot evaluation over either pure architecture alone. The intuition: SSM layers act as an efficient, general-purpose sequence mixer for the bulk of the network, while the sparse attention layers function as a precise retrieval mechanism, preventing the fixed-size recurrent state from being forced to compress every last detail of a long context into a single vector — offloading the specific, occasional cases where exact, unbounded lookup genuinely matters.

7. Where the Three Lineages Converge

Zooming out, these architectures didn’t emerge from one lineage — they trace back to three genuinely distinct starting points, and the striking thing about the current moment is how thoroughly those separate lineages have converged mathematically:

State space models started from continuous-time dynamical systems and Kalman filtering. Linear attention started as a direct efficiency modification of Transformer attention. Recurrent networks started from the classic LSTM, decades older than either. And yet Mamba-2’s SSD theorem proves SSMs and masked linear attention are mathematical duals; RetNet and GLA borrow directly from the SSM playbook of data-dependent state transitions; HGRN2 borrows its outer-product state expansion straight from linear attention; xLSTM’s mLSTM variant uses the same chunkwise parallel training strategy that powers RetNet and GLA. The boundaries between “this is an RNN,” “this is attention,” and “this is a state space model” are no longer architectural categories so much as three different lenses on the same underlying computation.

Conclusion

The impossible triangle — training parallelism, cheap constant-time inference, and Transformer-competitive quality, all at once — has, in a meaningful sense, been solved. Not through a single clever trick, but through a convergent set of ideas that keep reappearing across independently-developed architectures: exponential and data-dependent gating to control what gets remembered, outer-product and matrix-valued state expansion to grow memory capacity without exploding parameter count, multi-scale decay to let different parts of a network specialize in different time horizons, and — underlying all of it — hardware-aware chunkwise algorithms that treat the GPU’s memory hierarchy as a design constraint from day one, not an implementation afterthought.

Mamba-2, xLSTM, RetNet, and Gated Linear Attention aren’t best understood as efficient approximations of the Transformer, trading quality for speed. They’re closer to a genuine theoretical unification of recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based computation — three lineages that turn out, on close mathematical inspection, to have been converging toward the same place all along. As context lengths keep growing — across language, genomics, audio, and vision — these sub-quadratic, state-expanded architectures look less like a clever alternative to the Transformer, and more like its direct successor.
art-sub-16:
A Historical Crossroads for the Transformer

Since 2017, the Transformer has been the default engine behind nearly every major advance in natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems. Its core mechanism — dot-product self-attention — is also its Achilles’ heel: computing attention requires building an N×N matrix of pairwise token comparisons, and both the time and memory cost of that matrix grow quadratically, O(N²), with sequence length N.

For short sequences this is a non-issue. But push toward the sequences the real world actually produces — a user’s multi-year purchase history, a full-length legal document, a high-resolution image treated as a sequence of patches — and the quadratic term stops being a footnote and starts being the reason the model simply can’t run.

Linear attention is the response: drop the non-linear softmax, lean on the associativity of matrix multiplication, and reduce both time and memory to O(N) — linear instead of quadratic. This piece looks at two of the most consequential recent results in that line of work: LinRec, which solved the long-standing quadratic bottleneck in sequential recommender systems, and LION, which cracked open bidirectional sequence modeling — letting linear-time architectures finally match Transformers at tasks like vision and masked language modeling, where a model needs to see both past and future context at once.

Along the way, we’ll zoom out to the broader taxonomy of linear-attention research — approximation-based methods, state space models, gated linear RNNs, and hybrids — to see where these two results sit in a much larger, fast-moving map.

Why Standard Attention Falls Apart on Long Sequences

It helps to be precise about why this breaks down, because the failure isn’t just “it’s slow.” There are two distinct problems.

The first is arithmetic. When sequence length N is much larger than the embedding dimension d (a regime symbolized N ≫ d), computing the intermediate N×N matrix QKᵀ eats GPU memory fast and slows processing to a crawl. A user history of a few thousand interactions, or a document of tens of thousands of tokens, can push this cost past what any single accelerator can hold — long before you’d expect based on the model’s actual parameter count.

The second is subtler, and it’s a modeling problem, not just a systems problem. The softmax function has a strong tendency toward attention concentration — it pushes most of the probability mass onto a small number of high-scoring positions. In long sequences, this means the model’s attention naturally clusters around a few local, recent positions, while genuinely important signals sitting further back in the history get systematically starved of attention weight. The model isn’t just slow on long sequences — it’s structurally biased against remembering them well.

Earlier fixes — fixed sparse patterns, external memory modules, low-rank approximations like Linformer — chipped away at the compute problem but often introduced new complexity (extra projection steps, additional hyperparameters) and, in sensitive applications like recommendation, measurable accuracy drops. What was missing was an architecture that could drop the quadratic cost without giving up the mathematical properties that made dot-product attention work well in the first place.

LinRec: A Renaissance for Long-Term Sequential Recommenders

Why recommenders are a uniquely hard long-sequence problem

Sequential recommender systems (SRS) are the invisible infrastructure behind e-commerce, social feeds, and streaming platforms — their job is to predict what a user does next, based on everything they’ve done before. In industrial deployments, “everything they’ve done before” can mean thousands of clicks, views, and purchases spanning months or years. Researchers use a simple ratio to flag when a sequence counts as genuinely “long-term”: when the ratio of sequence length to embedding dimension, N/d, exceeds roughly 1.5, the standard quadratic-attention playbook starts to break down.

Transformer-based recommenders like SASRec, BERT4Rec, and FDSA set strong accuracy benchmarks — but their quadratic cost caps them at sequences of only a few dozen items in practice. That’s a real constraint: a lot of genuinely useful signal about a user’s preferences lives further back than a few dozen interactions ago.

Introduced at SIGIR 2023, LinRec (L2-Normalized Linear Attention) targets this gap directly, with a design that goes well beyond simply “removing softmax.”

Three structural changes, not one algebraic trick

LinRec’s authors didn’t just drop softmax and call it a day — they diagnosed exactly what breaks when you do that naively, and fixed each failure point individually.

1. Reordering the matrix multiplication. Using the associativity of matrix multiplication, LinRec computes Q(KᵀV) instead of (QKᵀ)V. The key insight: multiply K and V together first, producing a small d×d matrix, and only then multiply by Q. The N×N intermediate matrix never gets built at all. This single reordering takes complexity from O(N²d) down to O(Nd²) — genuinely linear in sequence length N.

2. Dual L2 normalization. Here’s the problem removing softmax creates: softmax’s normalization is what keeps attention values numerically bounded. Strip it out naively and you risk exploding gradients as networks get deep. LinRec’s fix is to normalize Q row-wise and K column-wise, both using the L2 norm — a targeted substitute that controls vector magnitudes and keeps training numerically stable without reintroducing the expensive softmax computation.

3. A non-linear activation before the dot product. Pure linear operations have limited capacity to model complex patterns. LinRec adds a non-linear activation (such as ELU) to Q and K before the attention computation. This does double duty: it restores some of the non-linear expressiveness that a purely linear reformulation would otherwise lose, and it introduces a form of intelligent sparsity — letting the model focus on the most behaviorally relevant parts of a user’s history instead of spreading attention thin.

A regularization effect, almost by accident

One of the more interesting theoretical findings in the LinRec paper is what its normalization and activation choices do to the shape of the resulting attention matrix. Softmax tends to produce sharp, concentrated attention distributions — exactly the concentration effect described earlier, where old-but-important signals get crowded out. LinRec’s combination of dual normalization and activation naturally produces a smoother attention distribution instead, spreading relevance more evenly across a long history. In effect, the architecture change built specifically for computational efficiency turns out to also act as a regularizer against the very attention-concentration problem that made long sequences hard to model in the first place.

The numbers

LinRec was evaluated on two very different benchmark datasets — ML-1M (movie ratings, naturally dense interaction patterns) and Gowalla (location check-ins, highly sparse) — using the standard recommender metrics Recall@10, MRR, and NDCG@10.

On ML-1M, swapping a conventional linear attention mechanism (LT) for LinRec inside the same SASRec backbone produced statistically significant gains (p < 0.05) across every metric: 7.1–9.6% improvement on Recall@10, 9.6–28.0% on MRR, and 8.8–21.7% on NDCG@10 — all without adding extra parameters.

The sparse Gowalla dataset told a consistent story, with LinRec again outperforming both the plain linear-transformer baseline and an alternative efficient-attention variant (EA) across all three metrics. The takeaway: unlike prior linear approximations that traded away learning quality to hit linear complexity, LinRec’s careful reconstruction of the attention conditions — reordering, dual normalization, and non-linearity — preserves the mathematical properties that made dot-product attention effective, while still running in linear time.

LION: Cracking Open Bidirectional Sequence Modeling

The piece linear attention was still missing

LinRec solved long-sequence efficiency for causal architectures — models that only look backward, which is exactly what a next-item recommender needs. But a huge class of problems needs the opposite: bidirectional modeling, where a model has to consider both past and future context simultaneously. Masked language modeling (think BERT) and vision transformers both work this way — a masked word’s meaning depends on words after it too; a patch of an image depends on the whole image, not just what came “before” it in some arbitrary scan order.

State space models like Mamba, and various linear transformers, had already shown they could match Transformer-quality causal modeling at a fraction of the cost, behaving like RNNs with constant memory footprints and linear time complexity. But bidirectional versions of these efficient architectures — Vision Mamba, Hydra, and similar attempts — hit a wall: to see both directions, they generally had to process the sequence twice (once forward, once backward) and merge the results, which badly hurt training throughput compared to a fully parallelizable softmax Transformer. Efficient at inference, slow to train — not a great trade.

LION (Linear attention for efficient bIdirectiOnal sequence modeliNg), accepted at NeurIPS 2025, is the first framework to resolve this cleanly.

Three mathematically equivalent forms — pick the one your hardware wants

The core theoretical contribution of LION is a proof that a bidirectional linear-attention function can be expressed in three completely equivalent mathematical forms. Because they’re provably equivalent, not just approximately similar, a model can switch between them depending on whether it’s training or serving, and depending on the hardware it’s running on:

  • Full Linear Attention Form — used during training. This form is fully parallelizable across GPU cores, giving LION training speeds competitive with softmax Transformers. This directly solves bidirectional SSMs’ historical weakness: slow training.

  • Bidirectional RNN Form — used at inference. Standard Transformers need a KV-cache that grows with sequence length; LION’s RNN form instead keeps a fixed-size memory footprint (scaling only with dimension d, not sequence length) and processes each token in constant time.

  • Chunkwise Parallel Form — a middle ground. Long sequences are split into chunks; attention runs fully parallel within each chunk, while information passes recurrently between chunks. This is the practical sweet spot for inference on memory-constrained hardware that still needs decent throughput.

The elegance here isn’t just having three options — it’s that they’re the same underlying function, proven equivalent, so switching between them costs nothing in terms of model quality. You get the training speed of a Transformer and the inference footprint of an RNN, from a single trained model.

A family of variants, organized around one dial: decay

LION functions less like a single architecture and more like a meta-model — a framework that a range of specific linear transformers can be derived from. To demonstrate this, the researchers built three concrete variants that differ mainly in how they handle a decay factor: how much weight recent versus distant information gets.

  • LION-LIT (no decay) — a direct bidirectional generalization of the original 2020 Linear Transformer. No filtering mechanism at all: full linear attention applies uniformly in both directions. Simplest of the three, but limited on complex language tasks that benefit from weighting recency.

  • LION-D (learnable, non-selective decay) — built on ideas from RetNet. A single decay parameter λ is learned during training but applied uniformly, independent of input content. This functions similarly to relative positional encoding, but more efficiently, weighting recent context more heavily by default.

  • LION-S (selective, input-dependent decay) — the flagship variant. Taking inspiration from Mamba’s continuous selective mechanism, LION-S computes a decay mask λᵢ dynamically, based on the actual content of each input token. This lets the model actively filter out noise and hold onto genuinely important information — the mechanism most directly responsible for LION’s strength on very long sequences.

Where LION actually wins

LION was evaluated across Tiny, Small, and Base model scales (roughly 5.5M to 21.7M parameters in its vision configurations), across three very different domains.

Computer vision (ImageNet-1K). Swapping standard attention blocks in a Vision Transformer for LION-S blocks — with no hyperparameter changes and no heavy data augmentation — produced results that beat other efficient SSM-based architectures at small scale and stayed highly competitive as scale increased:

At Small scale, the gap between LION-S and the full quadratic ViT-S baseline narrows to just 1.33 points. The more striking number is efficiency, not accuracy: LION-S trains up to 9× faster than Vision Mamba, and its cache-free inference runs dozens of times faster than KV-cache-dependent Transformers. In a knowledge-distillation setup based on DeiT, a distilled LION-S variant actually surpassed ViT-T outright, reaching 67.95% accuracy — a case where the efficient architecture didn’t just close the gap, it won.

Natural language processing (GLUE and C4). On masked language modeling and the GLUE benchmark, the Base LION-S model (110M parameters) reached an average GLUE score of 78.5 — a bit behind heavyweight baselines like BERT (80.6) or Hydra. But the trade-off is lopsided in LION’s favor on the efficiency side: over 2× faster training than Hydra, plus cache-free inference — a genuinely attractive trade for real-time or resource-constrained deployment, even if it isn’t yet a strict accuracy win.

Long Range Arena (LRA) — the real stress test. The hardest task in LRA is Path-X, which requires processing 16,384 tokens in a single sequence. Standard Transformers don’t just perform poorly here — they fail outright, reduced to random-guessing accuracy because the memory requirements are simply infeasible. LION (specifically LION-S and LION-D, initialized using HIPPO theory for stable long-range memory) solves Path-X with high stability. This is arguably the cleanest demonstration in the whole paper: LION’s long-context capability isn’t a side effect of clever engineering — it’s structurally built into the architecture, with no computational blow-up as sequence length grows.

The Bigger Map: Four Families of Linear Attention Research

LinRec and LION are two strong results, but they sit inside a much larger, fast-moving research landscape. Reference repositories tracking this space — Awesome-LA-Papers and the Awesome-Linear-Attention-Survey — organize the field into four broad families:

1. Approximation-based methods. The first generation of this idea — Performer, Luna, and similar architectures — tried to approximate softmax’s output directly, using deterministic or randomized kernels. Theoretically elegant, but in practice these approximations tended to cost real accuracy on tasks demanding precise logical reasoning, since they were fundamentally still trying to mimic softmax rather than replace its function outright.

2. State space models (SSMs) and the Mamba paradigm. Starting from linear time-invariant (LTI) state-space formulations, this line of work reached a peak with selective SSMs — Mamba and Mamba-2 — which make the state-transition dynamics depend on the actual input, rather than being fixed in advance. This input-dependent selectivity, implemented through continuous-time mathematics, is exactly the idea LION-S borrows for its dynamic decay mask.

3. Gated linear RNNs. Running in parallel to the SSM line, another branch of research went back to classic RNNs and stripped out the non-linear dependencies between consecutive hidden states — architectures like RWKV, HGRN, and xLSTM. Combining gating with linear (rather than non-linear) state transitions turns out to preserve full parallelizability during training, while giving these models a notable, largely unadvertised advantage: strong long-term modeling stability, and an inherent independence from needing explicit positional encoding schemes.

4. Hybrid architectures and distillation-based linearization. The most active current branch operates on a simple premise: no single architecture wins on every task. Block-level Transformer-SSM hybrids (Griffin, Jamba) mix both mechanisms within a single model, trading off generation quality against memory footprint at a fine-grained level. A related and increasingly important trend is linearization — techniques like Liger and LoLCATs that distill the knowledge already baked into a pretrained softmax model (say, a LLaMA-scale LLM) directly into a recurrent or linear-attention model, without a full, expensive retrain from scratch. This matters enormously for deployment: it offers a path to get giant, already-trained models running efficiently on constrained hardware, without redoing the original training investment.

Where These Threads Converge

Looking at LinRec and LION together against this broader taxonomy, a few genuinely cross-domain patterns stand out — places where problems that used to be tackled in separate research silos are now converging on very similar mathematical formulations.

Dynamic memory and continuous learning. Recent work on test-time memory (architectures that update their internal state during inference, not just during training) lines up naturally with what a production recommender like LinRec fundamentally needs: the ability to track real-time shifts in a user’s preferences without requiring a full model retrain every time behavior changes. Recurrent architectures with built-in test-time adaptability are a natural fit for that requirement.

Freedom from positional encoding in unstructured data. A shared, somewhat underappreciated advantage across recurrent linear models like LION is that they don’t need the heuristic positional-encoding schemes Transformers rely on — the hidden state itself implicitly carries positional and sequential information as it accumulates. That makes these models naturally good at length extrapolation (handling sequences longer than anything seen in training), and it matters for genuinely variable-length or non-sequential data — 3D point clouds, for instance — where imposing an artificial position scheme was always somewhat awkward to begin with.

Sustainability as a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought. Replacing quadratic architectures with linear ones like LION has a direct, measurable effect on data-center power consumption — increasingly one of the central constraints on how far AI systems can scale at all. The combination of large memory reductions and multi-fold speedups these architectures deliver isn’t just a performance story; it’s becoming part of the case for how the next generation of large-scale, always-on systems (recommenders included) get built responsibly.

Conclusion and Strategic Outlook

The shift away from quadratic dot-product attention toward linear and recurrent formulations has stopped being a matter of engineering elegance and become something closer to a survival requirement for systems that need to scale. LinRec demonstrates that careful, targeted algebraic restructuring — reordering the multiplication, adding dual L2 normalization, reintroducing non-linearity where it’s actually needed — can bring industrial-scale, ultra-long-sequence recommenders up to full accuracy without sacrificing the nuanced behavioral signal that makes recommendations useful in the first place.

LION, in turn, shows that a single model can genuinely have it both ways: full Transformer-level parallelization during training, and constant-memory RNN-style efficiency during inference — breaking what had been a stubborn, seemingly structural trade-off for bidirectional sequence models specifically. That its three forms are provably equivalent, not just empirically similar, is what makes the result durable rather than a clever one-off trick.

Zooming out, the trend lines across the broader taxonomy point in a consistent direction: no single pure architecture — not Transformers, not SSMs, not gated RNNs — looks likely to dominate every task going forward. The field is visibly consolidating around hybrid designs, distillation-based linearization of already-trained models, and selective, input-dependent gating as the shared toolkit. And the fact that vision, language, and industrial recommendation research are now converging on strikingly similar mathematical formulations suggests something bigger than any one architecture: a genuinely unified, cross-domain approach to efficient sequence modeling — one built to scale toward the kind of long-context, always-on, resource-conscious AI systems the next decade will actually demand.
